shapes.text: Ling 285Human Language and TechnologyLecture 19Neuron  NNs  LLMs  Agents!!!!

Khalil Iskarous
Department of Linguistics
University of Southern California

LLM: dynamical system with
many vectors in, 1 decision vector out

Agentic system:
a graph of LLMs

The agents (LLMs) speak to each other in English, but they are multilingual in human and computer languages!!!!!!!

Inference: inner products
Learning: SGD + DP

speakerNotes:
Click 1: one neuron — a vector comes in, one number comes out (an inner product).
Click 2: a small network, layers 4-3-4-5 — each W turns a vector into a vector; the last layer is a decision vector.
Click 3: an LLM — 15 token vectors go in at the bottom, pass up through 5 layers of W's (6 colours = 6 kinds of W), and the top yields vector 16: a probability distribution over the next token.
Click 4: agentic systems — several LLMs wired into a graph, with a critic/revise loop.
Click 5: the two operations under everything: inference is inner products; learning is SGD plus dynamic programming (backprop).

shapes.text: An LLM’s task, the prediction of the next word is difficult. So difficult that it need many many layers of its dynamical system. But it also needs, in each layer, many pallel heads, where each head is a different expert, and in each layer, all the knowledge from different heads/experts is brought together to generate improved representations x. Then the same things is done yet again in the next layer.
Dynamical System: A rule for data, fed back to itself
fed back in, again and again
xn+1 = xn + h·vn      vn+1 = vn − h·xn+1
x and v take turns. Step by step, the rule draws a cosine.
Based on time variation in speech production, Jordan proposed a marriage of NNs and Dynamical sysyems that after 30+ years of tinkering became the LLM ☺️
LLM: the layer is the rule
Each layer applies its W's to every vector. Depth plays the role of time: one number, followed up the layers, is a curve, just not a cosine.

speakerNotes:
Click 1: the machine. Numbers go in, a rule acts, numbers come out, and the output is fed back in as the next input. The numbers shown are the oscillator's first step (x0 = 1, v0 = 0, h = 2π/16).
Click 2: the harmonic oscillator, played automatically. x and v take turns: x(n+1) uses v(n); then v(n+1) uses the new x(n+1). The orange arrows show this interleaving for the first two steps. The dots trace a cosine (x) and a minus-sine (v). (This interleaved update is the symplectic Euler rule, which is why the curve does not spiral out.)
Click 3: Jordan's 1986 network. Plan and state units feed the hidden layer, which feeds the output; the output is copied back into the state units, which also keep a decaying copy of themselves (the small loops). Same W's every step.
Click 4: an LLM drawn as layers only, with the 15 vectors between them.
Click 5, played automatically: the rule is applied layer by layer (W1 ... W5). Follow one number in each vector up through the stack and you get a curve, built point by point as in the oscillator, but not sinusoidal. Depth is the LLM's time. One difference to point out: in the oscillator and the Jordan net the same rule is reused every step; in an LLM each layer has its own W.

shapes.text: The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ____
an image, cut into 16 patches, read row by row
a protein (insulin, B chain), read as 15 amino acids
The LLM only ever sees vectors. Words, sounds, pixels, molecules: one machine, one question: what is x₁₆?

speakerNotes:
Start: just 15 vectors and an empty 16th slot. Ask: vectors of what?
Click 1: a sentence, cut into 15 words; each x_i points at one word. x_16 is the missing word.
Click 2: the words go; now a spectrogram, cut into 15 frames. Same x_i, now pointing at frames. x_16 is the next frame.
Click 3: now an image cut into 16 patches, read row by row. x_16 is the missing bottom-right patch.
Click 4: now a folded protein (insulin B chain, FVNQHLCGSHLVEAL) read as a sequence of amino acids. x_16 is the next residue (it is Y).
Click 5: the takeaway: the machine only sees vectors; the sequence can come from anywhere.

shapes.text: Which sequences can be English words?
A simple syllable in English can have a consonant then a vowel then a consonant
Only certain sequences are allowed before the vowel and after the vowel
A long word is a chain of syllables: t·l is fine across a break (At·lan·tic), but tl cannot start a syllable

speakerNotes:
Click 1: twenty one-syllable words, each a single consonant, a single vowel, a single consonant (consonants dark, vowel red, silent e grey).
Click 2: the CVC rule.
Click 3: clusters. Top: real words with clusters (blue). Bottom: an impossible twin (red, starred). Many twins use the same letters in the other order (flat/*lfat, help/*hepl, lamp/*lapm): order matters, and it mirrors around the vowel.
Click 4: only certain sequences are allowed before and after the vowel.
Click 5: many-syllable words. Atlantic, athlete, admit contain t-l, th-l, d-m, which are impossible as onsets (*tlantic, *thlete, *dmit) but fine across a syllable break. ng can end a syllable (ring) but never start one (*ngapkin).
Click 6: a word is a chain of syllables, each obeying the same rules.

shapes.text: How phonotactic knowledge can be revealed through GPT learning
Each is the start of an English word. Guess the next letter.
l r a e i o
l, r or a vowel    never *spn
r l a e i o u
r, l or a vowel    never *bn
r l a e i o u
r, l or a vowel    never *fn
a e i o u r
Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆. A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling.

speakerNotes:
Let students guess first. Notice how fast they agree, and how the agreement changes from item to item.
Click 1: likely next letters (green), the rule, and one impossible continuation (red).
  The contrast to draw out: after a vowel (fa_) almost anything can follow; at the start of a word the choices narrow sharply (sp_, b_, f_: r, l or a vowel), and after skr_ or m_ only a vowel is possible.
  bram_ almost forces b (bramble), but a new syllable could also start there.
Click 2: guessing the next letter is exactly the next-token game. A GPT that only ever plays it learns these patterns: its predicted distribution is flat after fa_ and sharply peaked after skr_.

shapes.text:
Now we will build an LLM together by designing
an agentic system that learns the 
knowledge of English syllables that you have!!!!
Learning = nudging the weights so these guesses get better.
Today: the same idea, but the signal holds words, sounds and pictures.

speakerNotes:
Click 1: Here is a sentence the model is reading. The last word is hidden.
Click 2: Each earlier word gives a clue about the hidden word. These arcs are the interdependencies you already know about.
Click 3: The model doesn't know the answer. It spreads its bets: egg, nut, code.
Click 4: Learning just means nudging the weights, so that next time the right word gets a bigger bet.
Click 5: Today nothing about this changes. The only change is that the signal now holds sounds and pictures too.

shapes.text: The problem: not everything comes in words
Question: how do we turn all three into rows of vectors?

speakerNotes:
Click 1: Text is easy. It already comes as a row of pieces, so each piece can become a vector.
Click 2: Speech is different. It is air pressure going up and down in time. There are no words in it.
Click 3: An image is a grid of light. Again, no words.
Click 4: So the first job is a conversion. Everything has to become a row of vectors, because that is all the LLM can read.

shapes.text: Speech: slice time into short frames
One second of speech becomes 50 vectors, in a row, in time order.

speakerNotes:
This is a small piece of speech.
Click 1: We cut it into short slices. Each slice is about 20 milliseconds long.
Click 2: The slices go through a speech encoder. It is a network that was trained on lots of audio.
Click 3: Out comes one vector per slice. The shading just suggests different numbers.
Click 4: So one second of speech becomes 50 vectors in time order. That is a row, just like a sentence.

shapes.text: Images: cut the picture into patches

One vector per patch.
Real systems use patches of 14 to 16 pixels, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.

speakerNotes:
Here is our picture: an egg in a pan.
Click 1: We cut it into a grid of small squares. They are called patches.
Click 2: We lay the patches out in a row, in reading order. Now the picture is a sequence, like a sentence.
Click 3: The patches go through a vision encoder.
Click 4: Out comes one vector per patch.
Click 5: Our grid is 4 by 4 to keep it simple. Real systems use tiny patches, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.

shapes.text: Same game as before. Now some of the clues come from other senses.

speakerNotes:
Now we put everything in one row.
Click 1: First the image patches.
Click 2: Then the speech slices.
Click 3: Then the words, with the last one hidden.
Click 4: The old clues are still there: earlier words help guess the hidden word.
Click 5: The new thing. A patch showing an egg, and the sound of cracking, also help. These are cross-modal dependencies.
Click 6: The game is exactly the same as before. Guess the hidden piece. Some of the clues now come from other senses.

shapes.text: A new example: three cute puppies
The phrase, spoken. Time runs left to right; frequency goes up.
Three views of one event. Training puts them in one row.

speakerNotes:
A new example, which we will use for the rest of the training story.
Click 1: A picture of three puppies.
Click 2: As before, it is cut into patches: 3 rows of 6, so 18 patches.
Click 3: The same phrase, spoken. This is a spectrogram. Time runs left to right. Higher up means higher frequency. Darker means more energy.
Click 4: Here is where each word sits in time. Each thin column of the spectrogram is a frame.
Click 5: And the words themselves, as text.
Click 6: Three views of one event. In training, all three go into one row, and the model plays the hide-and-guess game on it.
(The speech was made with a speech synthesizer, an MBROLA diphone voice.)

shapes.text: Training example 1: predict the next word

Truth: puppies.
The model bet 0.85 on it, so the nudge to the weights is small.

speakerNotes:
This is the game from the start of the lecture, now on a three-sense row.
Click 1: The row. First the picture, then the sound, then the words. The last word is hidden.
Click 2: Suppose the model only had the words "three cute". Many endings fit: kittens, puppies, babies. Its bets are spread out.
Click 3: Now add the clues from the other senses. The picture shows puppies. The sound contains the spoken word "puppies". The bet piles up on "puppies".
Click 4: The true word is revealed. The model is graded on how much it bet on the truth. It bet a lot, so the error is small, and the weights move only a little.

shapes.text: Training example 2: predict a sound frame
Earlier frames: the voice and the formants carry on.
Words: the next sound is the vowel of “pup”.
Picture: puppies, which backs up the words.

speakerNotes:
Now the hidden piece is a piece of sound.
Click 1: The row is reordered: picture, then words, then sound. This is like teaching the model to speak a sentence it was given. The sound is predicted frame by frame, left to right. The frames to the right are not heard yet. The orange frame is the one to guess.
Click 2: The first clue comes from earlier frames. The speaker's voice and the formants change smoothly, so the last few frames say a lot about the next one.
Click 3: The words say which sound should come next. Here it is the vowel in "pup".
Click 4: The picture shows puppies. It backs up the words. It is a weaker clue here.
Click 5: A frame is a column of numbers: how much energy there is in each frequency band. We show 16 bands. The model's guess is close but not exact. The error is how far apart each number is.
Click 6: That error is what nudges the weights.
Note: some systems predict a code for each frame instead of the raw numbers. That is the "talking back" idea at the end.

shapes.text: Training example 3: predict a picture patch
Earlier patches: background above, two puppies to the left.
Words: “three” = one more puppy; “puppies” = dog ears.
Biggest error: the colour. No clue said the third puppy is dark.

speakerNotes:
Last, the hidden piece is a piece of the picture.
Click 1: The row is reordered again: words, then sound, then the picture. This is like teaching the model to draw what it was told. The patches are predicted in reading order. The patches not yet drawn are faded. The gray patch is the one to guess.
Click 2: Earlier patches give the first clue. Above is background. To the left are two puppies, so the model has seen what a puppy here looks like.
Click 3: The words help in a different way. "Three" says a third puppy must appear, and only two have been drawn. "Puppies" says to expect dog ears.
Click 4: The sound carries the same words. It is a backup for the text.
Click 5: The guess is a blurry puppy ear, in the average colour of the first two puppies. The truth is a dark puppy.
Click 6: So the biggest error is the colour. Nothing in the words, the sound or the earlier patches said the third puppy would be dark. That error nudges the weights.
Note: only systems that also produce pictures are trained this way. Systems that only read pictures usually skip this step.

shapes.text: Every piece can be the hidden one
Backs up which word is said

Outlined: the same sense. It says how the signal continues.
The other senses say what the thing is.

speakerNotes:
A summary of the three training examples.
Clicks 1 to 3: One row per kind of hidden piece. Each cell is the clue that one sense gives.
Click 4: Look at the outlined diagonal. Clues from the same sense mostly say how the signal continues: grammar, smooth formants, fur and background. Clues from the other senses mostly say what the thing is: puppies, three of them.
That is why training on all three senses together helps. Each sense fills gaps the others leave.

shapes.text: Talking back, and the big picture
Sound compressed into codes: new “words” in the vocabulary
The model predicts the next code, like the next word.

What is new
1.  A shared currency: everything becomes vectors in one row
2.  Data where the senses appear together
3.  A schedule that protects what was already learned
What stays the same:  find the dependencies in the signal.

speakerNotes:
So far the model only reads pictures and sound. How does it speak?
Click 1: Sound is compressed into discrete codes. Each code is like a new word added to the vocabulary.
Click 2: The model predicts the next code exactly as it predicts the next word. Same game again.
Click 3: A decoder turns the codes back into a sound wave.
Click 4: The big picture. Three things are new: a shared currency of vectors, data where the senses appear together, and a schedule that protects what was learned. The learning rule is unchanged: find the dependencies in the signal. The signal just got wider.
